title: Troubleshooting with dig, curl, and traceroute

questions.prompt: Match each tool to the layer it helps diagnose.
questions.explanation: dig checks DNS, traceroute maps the path, curl probes the application, and curl -w breaks down where the time goes.

questions.prompt: How does traceroute discover each hop?

options.text: By sending probes with increasing TTLs and reading the ICMP Time Exceeded replies
By asking DNS for the list of routers
By opening a TCP connection to every router
By broadcasting to the whole internet

questions.explanation: Each probe's TTL is increased by one; the router where TTL hits 0 returns ICMP Time Exceeded, revealing itself one hop at a time.

questions.prompt: A traceroute shows '* * *' at hop 6, but hops 7, 8, and the destination all reply. What does this indicate?

options.text: Hop 6 just isn't replying to probes; the path is fine
The network is definitely broken at hop 6
The destination server returned a 500 error

questions.explanation: Intermediate routers often ignore or rate-limit probes, producing '* * *'. Since later hops and the destination respond, the path works.

questions.prompt: The dig status meaning 'this name does not exist' is ____.
questions.explanation: NXDOMAIN means the queried name doesn't exist; SERVFAIL means the resolver failed to get an answer.

questions.prompt: Which are good uses of curl for diagnosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: curl -I to see the status code and headers quickly
curl -v to inspect the TLS handshake and full exchange
curl --resolve to test a specific backend IP, bypassing DNS
curl to map every router on the path to the server

questions.explanation: curl inspects HTTP/TLS and can bypass DNS with --resolve. Mapping routers on the path is traceroute's job, not curl's.

items.text: traceroute — can packets reach the host?
curl — does the service respond correctly?

questions.explanation: Work in layer order: resolve the name, then check the path, then probe the application — each tool rules a layer in or out.
